cultivar: Zaobaijian, Jiangnan and locally bred Yongchuan Xiuya cultivars
processing: One bud with one leaf is pan-fixed, rolled by hand into a ball, tossed to shed moisture, then shaped into needles by rubbing the leaf between the palms in a pan at 60–70 °C and baked to about 6% moisture. The shaping step gives the tea its tight, straight form.
harvest_season: Picked at one bud with one leaf; as with other fine needle greens, spring is the usual and most valued season.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine, straight needles of fresh emerald green, with down showing at the tips.
appearance_wet: Tender, bright leaf ranging from green to light yellow.
taste_profile: Fresh and mellow with a returning sweetness, under a rich, lasting, tender aroma.

brewing.notes: General guidance for needle greens rather than a local rule: a glass shows off the needles, and water around 80 °C keeps the fresh aroma from turning flat.

vintage_note: Sold as a fresh green tea from the current harvest and best within about a year; cold storage is the recommended way to keep it. Check the harvest date and the registered Yongchuan Xiuya mark, since the name is a geographical indication trademark held by the district tea association.
description:
Yongchuan Xiuya is a needle-shaped green tea from Yongchuan in western Chongqing, grown across five ranges: Yunwu, Yinshan, Bayue, Jishan and Huanggua. Unlike most famous Chinese greens it has no old legend. It was designed by a research institute in the twentieth century.

The character of the tea comes from the shaping. After fixing and rolling, the maker straightens the strips in a warm pan and rubs them between the palms, letting them drop through the fingers again and again until they are tight, straight and showing down at the tip.

The cup is a clear emerald with a rich, tender aroma and a fresh, mellow taste that turns sweet afterwards. Measurements report relatively high amino acid levels, which fits that soft savoury sweetness. Keep the water cool and it stays that way.

The institute behind it also bred cultivars and released more than 20 other fine teas, so you may meet the name next to newer products. Look for the current harvest and keep the tea in the fridge once opened.
history:
The tea was developed by the tea research institute of the then Sichuan Academy of Agricultural Sciences, now part of the Chongqing academy. Accounts differ on the start, giving 1959 for its first production and 1963 for its creation. Zhu De is said to have praised it, and in 1964 the tea scholar Chen Chuan gave it the name Yongchuan Xiuya.

The tea went through stages of development and standardisation, won repeated Sichuan provincial tea appraisals, and was named a famous tea by the Ministry of Agriculture in 1989. Its processing method received a national invention patent in 2004.

The Yongchuan Xiuya trademark was approved in 2011 and issued to the district tea association. In 2019 it entered China's national agricultural brand catalogue.
